title: Four Sources of Grief
paragraphs: Socrates, the thinker par excellence, stands trial in the Greek court of law. The charge against him is that he instigated the youth against the state by his speeches. A group of three persons raise a furore proposing and seconding those charges in the court. These three persons-Anytus, Lichen and Meletus-level charges against Socrates which are in the nature of contempt of the great thinker.

Anytus: Seething volcano! Turbulent ocean! More terrible than all these is Socrates! ... Weapon of Wisdom! All the world would surrender to this missile, it is said!... If that weapon were to be manufactured in Greece, we would not be able to raise our heads, Meletus! What do you say, Lichen?

Lichen: I am a sculptor who carves God out of stone...! Once even this Socrates was a sculptor like me! But now he has metamorphosed into a sculptor of thoughts! It’s all right! After the three of us - me who create God out of stones, Meletus the poet who with his Midas touch gives divine shapes to bundles of imagination, and a political genius like you - once we have colluded together..., Socrates is nothing more than a worthless particle upon an ocean, isn’t he, Anytus...!

Meletus: Hurray, Lichen! Kudos... ! Only as long as people are like donkeys would they patiently bear the burden of falsehoods we place on their backs! Only if they are blind will they follow the way we show! We must put an end to him before he succeeds in opening the intellectual eyes of the masses who dare not
These were the barbs directed at a peerless man of wisdom and a revolutionary thinker, which constitute an attempt at disgracing Socrates.

India’s first Prime Minister, Nehru, who ruled for 17 long years, was hailed by all sections of the society - right from the common men to the elite. Here is a poem composed in the form of the grief of the rose which he sported on his coat on the death of Nehru, the light of Asia and the white dove of peace.
The nobel one! The man of principles! Where is that Death which robbed us of you?
Today, you took me and put me near your heart. But you have left me and gone far away. Is it fair?
You lent honey to my petals. Don’t you remember as to how I reciprocated that?
Has your heart turned into a stone, Depriving me of my joy overflowing?

On hearing the dirge, the other flowers approached the rose. Finding it in the flood of tears and is about to faint Jasmine went close and asked: “What Rose, why do you keep crying so long? A good person lived for the nation to benefit from. A munificent person lived to embrace us all, Could we ever get him back? Stop your wailing. The queen of flowers! Do smile.”

The Tamiḻ race stands tall today with pride and self-esteem thanks to the efforts of Periyār. When Periyār breathed his last, the Tamiḻs all over the world felt completely dispirited which is reflected in the following lines.
As a volcano, As a scorching fire, As a thunder striking terror among the foes,

As a burning torch of ethnic pride, As a billhook felling things disgraceful, As an Ingarsal refuting the very divinity, As a Socrates who never minced words, As a Voltaire in questioning things, Did our Periyār live his life! Behold him lying on the lap of death! He didn’t die young, a full life had he lived though If Taj Mahal were to be engulfed by the earth, Would we comfort ourselves saying, “Well, it was an old building?” Would we bear if the Big Temple of Tanjavur were to fall Saying it is an aged structure? Like these unforgettable monuments Periyār too has history made!
An emotion of this kind is what Tolkāppiyar calls decline (acaivu) that would cause grief and distress.

(Poverty had driven the purāṇic Nallataṅkāḷ and quite a number of mothers of the modern age as well to either sell the children begotten by them to eke out a living or drown them in a pond or river only to follow suit, later. The flooding tears at such spectacles of poverty constitute the sentiment of weeping.)
> The four inexorable sources of grief are > Contempt, deprivation, decline in stature and indigence.
